evidence: src/infrastructure/server.ts builds InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository, injects them into OrderService and CatalogueService, and mounts controller.router() and then errorMiddleware.
src/infrastructure/error-middleware.ts: errorMiddleware is the only place that maps NotFoundError to 404, DomainError to 400, and anything else to 500.
src/infrastructure/order-controller.ts: every route is wrapped in asyncRoute, which passes errors to next(error) so errorMiddleware handles them consistently.

src/infrastructure/order-controller.ts: isOrderStatus is built on the domain's orderStatuses, so the valid statuses are defined in one place; the check `typeof status !== "string" || !isOrderStatus(status)` is repeated in the GET /orders and PATCH /orders/:id/status routes (minor).

src/infrastructure/in-memory-repositories.ts: InMemoryProductRepository implements ProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository, both with the same Map-based storage pattern.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The infrastructure module is one cohesive concern: the adapter and composition layer for a single order-fulfilment API. in-memory-repositories.ts holds the persistence adapters for the domain repository ports. order-controller.ts is the HTTP adapter, delegating to OrderService and CatalogueService. error-middleware.ts is the single place where domain errors become HTTP status codes. server.ts is the composition root that wires them together. The module uses its own abstractions consistently: server.ts builds the app only from its sibling exports, and the controller hands every failure to errorMiddleware through next(error) instead of setting error statuses itself. Each rule lives in one place: the valid statuses come from the domain's orderStatuses, and the error-to-HTTP mapping exists only in errorMiddleware. Minor findings that don't fail the rubric: (1) OrderController.router() repeats the same status check inline in two routes, but both use one isOrderStatus helper, so this is not a duplicated invariant; (2) the class is named OrderController but also serves the /products routes, a narrow naming issue, not split concerns; (3) asyncRoute only catches errors thrown synchronously, but all current handlers are synchronous.
